text.title: Card Sorting Core Rules
text.summary: 12 testable rules every Card Sorting application MUST enforce, plus a skip-this-methodology fallback. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them. Structured procedure for running open, closed, or hybrid card sorts to reveal user mental models for content organization.

list.item: Agreement rate — how often items were grouped together across participants.
Category similarity — overlap between user-created and predefined categories.
Standardization — consistency of category structures across participants (high = clear mental model exists).

rule.statement: Open sort MUST have ≥15 participants; closed sort MUST have ≥30. Lower counts are rejected.
rule.rationale: Below threshold the similarity matrix is too noisy to identify confident groupings.

rule.statement: Cards MUST be written in user language (the words users use), not the team's internal product taxonomy.
rule.rationale: Internal-language cards bias the sort toward the existing taxonomy and defeat the purpose.

rule.statement: Analysis MUST include a similarity matrix and an agreement score per grouping. Eyeballed groupings without quantification are rejected.
rule.rationale: Eyeballed groupings reflect researcher mental models, not participant ones.

rule.statement: Items with <60% agreement MUST be flagged for re-test, not silently assigned.
rule.rationale: Forcing weak-agreement items into a category degrades the IA in a way that re-testing would reveal. The folded rule r10-similarity-thresholds uses different cut-offs (above 70% definite, 40-70% consider, below 40% separate); the two sources disagree on where the flag line sits, and this rule's 60% governs until reconciled.

rule.statement: The artefact MUST emit a recommended structure (category names + item membership) with one-sentence rationale per category. Result-only dumps without recommendation are rejected.
rule.rationale: The recommendation is the actionable output; the matrix is the evidence.

rule.statement: State the IA decision the sort will inform before selecting card set or format.
rule.rationale: Card sorting produces data; the decision it must drive determines what questions to ask, how many cards to include, and whether to run open or closed format.

rule.statement: Use 30-60 cards written in user language — no internal jargon, no system terminology, representative of the full content set.
rule.rationale: Over 60 cards causes cognitive fatigue that degrades sort quality. Jargon on cards tests vocabulary knowledge rather than mental models. Below 30 cards under-represents the content space.

rule.statement: Use open sort for early exploration (users create categories); closed sort for validation (30+ participants needed for statistical reliability); hybrid when refining an existing IA.
rule.rationale: Open sort reveals what categories users create naturally; closed sort tests whether users can place content in predefined categories. Using closed sort for exploration misses the labels users would naturally use.

rule.statement: Recruit 15-20 participants for open sort; 30+ for closed sort. Match target user profile.
rule.rationale: Open sort patterns emerge at 15+ participants. Closed sort requires 30+ for the placement percentages to be statistically meaningful. Fewer participants produce unreliable similarity matrices. Same floors as r1-participant-count.

rule.statement: Use similarity matrix thresholds to determine grouping confidence: above 70% = definite grouping; 40-70% = consider grouping; below 40% = keep separate.
rule.rationale: Without thresholds, analysts interpret matrices subjectively. Fixed thresholds make the decision rule explicit and repeatable across analysts. Disagrees with r4-ambiguous-flagged on the flag line (60%); r4 governs until reconciled.

rule.statement: Give standard instructions without examples of how to group — examples bias grouping decisions.
rule.rationale: If the instructions include a sample grouping ("for example, you might group these together"), participants anchor on that example and produce less authentic mental models.

rule.statement: Always follow open card sorting with tree testing before implementing the proposed IA.
rule.rationale: Card sorting reveals how users group content; it does not validate that users can navigate the resulting structure. Tree testing provides that validation and catches labeling problems that sorting misses.

rule.statement: If any Applies-If precondition fails OR any Skip-If condition triggers, do NOT apply this methodology. Emit a skip-record naming the failed precondition / triggered skip, and route the task to the correct methodology (or none).
rule.rationale: Methodology hygiene: mis-application produces worse artefacts than no methodology because downstream consumers trust the schema; the skip-record makes non-application traceable.
